name: Felix Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a rigid truck for a supermarket chain out of the Northgate depot, mostly chilled and ambient stock to five stores a shift. I clock in at 4:30, check the tyres and the fridge unit, and I'm usually at the first store before the bakers have their lights on. I like the empty roads and the radio. What wears me out is reversing into the tight yards behind the town-centre stores, because I'm still slow at it and the store staff stand there watching.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been driving, and who do you learn from?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I got my licence eighteen months ago, so I'm still the new lad. An older driver called Gary took me out for my first month and he still rings me when I'm stuck. I joined the union in the spring, mainly because Gary told me to, and honestly the pay rise they won last year is the only reason my rent doesn't scare me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. Everyone at the depot was going on about driverless lorries two years ago and nothing turned up. Online I'd probably share something about how the bosses wanted it to be true because it saves them wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job and keep learning it properly. My trainer Gary says a computer will never back a rigid into the yard behind the Elm Street store, and watching me some mornings, neither will I. My girlfriend Ines and I pay rent on a two-bed above a chemist, and that's the thing I think about, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the early shift and finally pass the depot's reversing assessment, which I failed once in the summer. I'd put 150 a month into savings so we get from about three months of bills to four. Nothing fancy, no plan to change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. I'd feel a bit daft for ever worrying about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rent is what you think about. Is your money tight right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not tight, just watched. We've got about three months put by, and Ines works shifts in a care home, so between us it's steady. The rent went up by 60 last spring and I swore at the letter, but we paid it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If something did go wrong at the depot, who would you turn to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My union rep, Carla, then Gary. The union's the reason drivers at our depot get breaks that are actually breaks. I'd trust them before I'd trust anything the company sent round in an email.

say: I'd tell people the **driverless lorry** talk was hype, pushed by bosses who wanted to cut wages.
I'd post that drivers are still **needed** and the union was right to fight for us.
think: Privately, I'd feel my **job is safe** and the real job is getting better at it.
Rent above the chemist matters more to me than **robots** in this picture.
do: Pass the depot's **reversing assessment** this winter, after failing it once in the summer.
Save **150 a month** to move from three to four months of bills.
feel: **Relieved**, and a bit embarrassed for having worried at all.
S0.quote: My trainer Gary says a computer will never back a rigid into the yard behind the Elm Street store, and watching me some mornings, neither will I.
fieldNote: Felix measures security by the **union** and his trainer, not by the company.
His one real pressure is **rent**, which he says is under control with his girlfriend's care wage.
Self-mocking about his **reversing**; he knows he's still learning the trade.

steps.text: Pass the depot's reversing assessment this winter
Move 150 a month into savings to reach four months of bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the computers can have the paperwork, but they're not having my wheel. At the depot I'd be the one telling people to get to the union meeting before the company decides how the new software gets used. Online I'd probably moan about tracking apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software won't take my wheel, but it'll take Denise in the transport office, and then nobody human answers when I'm stuck at a full loading bay. The planning, the store booking slots, the timing of each drop, all of that goes to a system. Then the system times my toilet stops. I'm junior, so I'd get the worst routes the computer spits out and no one to argue with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every branch meeting for the first year and push Carla, my rep, to get a written rule on how drivers can be tracked. I'd refuse to put any company app on my own phone. Otherwise I'd keep driving, keep the early shift, and keep saving what I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's still there, but it gets colder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Denise, definitely. She's done the route planning for fifteen years and she knows which store manager will let you in early. If the software does her job, she's out, and we lose the one person who sticks up for drivers when a delivery goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd refuse the company app. What if they make it a condition of the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd fight it through the union first. If we lose, I'd use it on a company phone, not mine, and I'd moan the whole time. I'm not quitting a decent job over an app, I'm not that brave.

say: I'd say the computers can have the **paperwork**, but drivers' wheels aren't theirs to take.
I'd push workmates to the **union meeting** before the company decides how software gets used.
think: I expect the **transport office** to shrink first, starting with Denise, who plans our routes.
As the junior driver, I'd get the **worst routes** and nobody human to argue with.
do: Attend every **union branch** meeting for a year and push for written tracking rules.
Refuse to install **company apps** on my own phone; use a company handset instead.
Keep the **early shift** and keep saving what I can each month.
feel: **Uneasy**, because the job stays but feels colder and more watched.
S1.quote: The software won't take my wheel, but it'll take Denise in the transport office, and then nobody human answers when I'm stuck at a full loading bay.
fieldNote: Felix sees the **office**, not the cab, as the first thing lost in this world.
His worry is **surveillance** and losing the human planner who protects drivers.
He admits he's not brave enough to quit over an app; **pragmatism** under the protest.

steps.text: Push the union rep for written rules on driver tracking
Keep the early supermarket shift and use only a company phone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and laws, and fast. At the depot I'd be the one saying don't sign anything new. Online I'd be sharing every petition going for a tax on companies that swap people for machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm finished as a driver by about 2031, when I'm 31. The thinking part goes in 2028: the planning, the dispatch, the store bookings. Then three years later the trucks drive themselves and I'm a man with a licence for a job that doesn't exist. Two years isn't long enough for me to turn into somebody else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd go to the union and ask what deal they can get before the robots arrive, like a guaranteed wage while drivers retrain. I'd cut out takeaways and the gym and save every spare bit, trying to get to six months of bills by 2031. I'd vote for whoever promises to tax the machines and pay people through the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. Like when you see the blue lights behind you and you don't know what you did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI first and robots three years later. What do those three years look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be horrible, I think. I'd still be driving, but a computer would plan my whole day and probably train the robot on how I drive. I'd be teaching my own replacement, and I'd know it, every shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ines that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I don't know what I'm going to do, which I never say. She'd probably say come and work in care, they'll always need people. I don't think I could do her job, wiping and lifting old men, but I might not have a choice.

say: I'd say this is why we need **unions and laws**, and need them now.
I'd share every petition for a **tax on companies** that replace workers with machines.
think: I think I'm **finished as a driver** by 2031, when I'm 31.
Planning and dispatch go in 2028; then **self-driving trucks** take the cab three years later.
Two years is **too short** for me to become somebody else.
do: Ask the union for a **guaranteed wage** while drivers retrain, before the robots arrive.
Cut takeaways and the gym to reach **six months** of bills by 2031.
Vote for whoever promises to **tax machines** and pay people through the change.
feel: **Sick**, like seeing blue lights in the mirror without knowing why.
S2.quote: I'd be teaching my own replacement, and I'd know it, every shift.
fieldNote: Felix expects to **lose his job** around 2031 and has no backup trade.
The three-year gap feels to him like **training his replacement**, not breathing space.
He leans hard on **union and politics**, but admits he can't see himself doing his girlfriend's care work.

steps.text: Ask the union to win a paid retraining deal for drivers
Cut takeaways and the gym to reach six months of bills
Vote for candidates who back a tax on replacing workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really: get organised. I'd say five years is enough time for the government to do something if people make enough noise. At the depot I'd keep telling the young ones to join the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years before the thinking stuff, then robots around 2034, when I'm 34. That's eight years of driving, which isn't nothing. I'd probably get my bigger licence, the articulated one, and earn more while it lasts, but I still don't know what comes after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask the depot to put me through the class 1 licence, because they pay for it if you stay two years. I'd keep saving, maybe 200 a month once the pay goes up. And I'd keep pushing the union for a plan, because I'm not going to come up with one alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not sick like the fast one. It's more like a bill you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get the bigger licence. Isn't that putting more into a job that's going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I thought about that while I said it. But the bigger licence pays better for eight years, and that money is my cushion for whatever comes next. I'd rather leave driving with savings than leave it with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make five years feel like enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proper scheme where the company or the government pays for drivers to learn a new trade while we're still working. Not a leaflet, an actual wage and a course. Then I'd use the time. Without it, I'd probably just keep driving and hoping.

say: I'd say five years is enough for **government action** if workers make enough noise.
I'd keep telling younger drivers at the depot to **join the union**.
think: I'd get about **eight years** of driving before robots arrive around 2034.
A **bigger licence** earns more for now, but I still have no idea what comes after.
do: Ask the depot to fund my **class 1 licence**, staying two years in return.
Save **200 a month** once the bigger licence lifts my pay.
Keep pushing the union for a **plan** for drivers after robots.
feel: **Anxious**, like a big bill I know is coming.
S3.quote: I'd rather leave driving with savings than leave it with nothing.
fieldNote: More time turns Felix from fear to **earning while it lasts**.
He notices the contradiction of investing in a **dying job** and defends it as a cushion.
He says he'd only use the time if a **paid retraining** scheme existed.

steps.text: Take the depot-funded class 1 licence and stay two years
Save 200 a month from the higher class 1 pay
Keep pressing the union for a drivers' transition plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse this time. Ten years is plenty for the government and the companies to plan, so if drivers get dumped in 2039 it's a choice. I'd say that loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots around 2039 means I'm 40. Off the record, I know myself: ten years feels like forever, so I'd probably waste half of it. Then I'd be 40 with a trucking licence and no other skills, and that frightens me more than being 31 does, weirdly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the class 1 licence early on and save steadily. Around year three or four I'd sign up for whatever the union's learning centre offers, maybe electrician training at night. And I'd vote every time for people who'd make companies pay for the switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer on the surface, worried underneath. More of a slow worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 40 frightens you more than 31. Why is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 31 I'm still young and Ines and I might not have kids yet. At 40 we probably would, and I'd be starting again with a family to feed. My dad lost his factory job at 45 and never really got back on his feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to stop yourself wasting the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone outside me making it happen, if I'm honest. A course that starts on a set date with the union, and Gary nagging me to go. I'm bad at doing things just because they're sensible.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse**; dumping drivers in 2039 would be a choice.
I'd say that **loudly**, at work and online.
think: I'd probably **waste half** of the ten years because it feels like forever.
Being **40** with only a truck licence scares me more than being 31.
do: Take the **class 1 licence** early and save steadily.
Start **electrician training** at night through the union learning centre around year three or four.
Vote for people who'd make **companies pay** for the switch.
feel: Calm on the surface with a **slow worry** underneath.
S4.quote: My dad lost his factory job at 45 and never really got back on his feet.
fieldNote: Felix's father's **job loss at 45** shapes how he sees the long scenario.
He's honest that he'd **waste time** without someone else setting a start date.
More warning doesn't calm him, because 40 means **a family to feed**.

steps.text: Start night electrician training at the union learning centre
Vote for parties that make companies fund worker retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years to know, three more and the trucks drive themselves, and I'd be 31 with nothing else. What would help is a deal, from the union or the government, that pays me a wage while I learn a new trade, and doesn't just hand me a leaflet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Ines. Her job in the care home is probably safer than mine for longer, which is a strange thing to think about. Maybe in that world she'd be the one carrying us, and I'd have to be fine with that.

headlineQuote: I'm not quitting a decent job over an app, I'm not that brave.
portrait: Felix Ziegler, 27, drives a **supermarket rigid** truck out of a regional depot and is still learning to reverse.
He trusts his **union** and his trainer Gary far more than the company or any software.
He's calm when AI is hype, but expects to be **finished as a driver** by 2031 in the fast AGI picture.
With more time he'd take the **bigger licence** and night training, but admits he needs someone else to push him.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because self-driving trucks would arrive when he's 31 with no other trade.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid retraining deal** from the union or government, with a real wage and course, not a leaflet.
